defaults.permitted_development: Planning permission is not usually required in England for an internal garage conversion where the work stays within the existing building and does not materially enlarge it. That answer can change where parking-retention conditions, external alterations or the creation of a separate dwelling are involved.

rules.height_rules: A straightforward internal conversion does not create a new householder height allowance. If the project raises the roof, adds an upper floor or rebuilds the garage, that external work needs to be assessed separately.
rules.depth_rules: The simplest route is a conversion wholly within the existing garage shell. Once the proposal projects outward, extends the footprint or enlarges the garage envelope, it moves into extension rules or a separate planning assessment.
rules.boundary_rules: Check whether an earlier permission required the garage or parking space to be retained. Highway-facing changes, new windows close to neighbours and estate or Article 4 controls can also make the planning answer more site-specific.
rules.roof_rules: If the conversion also changes the roof, separate roof or extension rules apply. A basic internal fit-out behind the existing roofline does not itself create a new roof planning allowance.
rules.materials_rules: Where the garage door is infilled, the new wall, window and detailing should look intentional and tie into the main house. Heritage controls and visible frontage changes usually call for the closest material match.

rules.permitted_development: The simplest garage conversion is an internal fit-out within the existing shell, which often does not need planning permission. The position changes quickly if the building is enlarged, rebuilt as part of the scheme or intended to operate as a separate home.

rules.height_rules: A pure conversion works within the existing envelope, so there is no separate garage-conversion height right. Once the roof is lifted, rebuilt or given an extra storey, treat that element as new external development.
rules.depth_rules: Depth is not the main test for a garage conversion. Staying within the existing footprint is the low-risk route, whereas any outward projection, linked enlargement or rebuild has to be considered under extension rules or a full planning route.
rules.boundary_rules: Boundary and frontage issues usually come from the external alterations rather than the internal fit-out. Also check whether an earlier permission required the garage or parking space to be retained as part of the approved layout.
rules.roof_rules: Roof changes are not part of the ordinary internal conversion question. Once the scheme includes a raised roof, dormer, rooflights on a sensitive elevation or other visible roof alteration, assess that work separately.
rules.materials_rules: The external treatment of a former garage opening matters more than the internal fit-out. A well-matched infill wall, window or entrance usually reads best, especially on a principal or street-facing elevation.

rules.permitted_development: Planning permission is not usually needed for a straightforward internal garage conversion, but enlarging the structure, changing the outside materially or creating separate living accommodation can move it outside the ordinary householder route.

rules.height_rules: Garage conversion does not create a fresh height allowance. The moment the scheme raises the roofline, adds a storey or materially rebuilds the structure, it needs to be assessed as extension or outbuilding development instead.
rules.depth_rules: A conversion inside the existing garage envelope is usually the easiest case. If the proposal extends the garage, pushes the front line out or adds linked built form, use the normal extension framework rather than assuming the conversion still stands alone.
rules.boundary_rules: The key local checks are often parking retention, frontage design and neighbour-facing openings. Even a simple garage-door infill can become a planning issue where earlier conditions controlled parking or the altered elevation is prominent.
rules.roof_rules: Garage conversion by itself does not open a separate roof right. Any proposal to lift, rebuild or materially alter the garage roof should be treated as external development in its own right.
rules.materials_rules: When a garage door is replaced, aim for an elevation that belongs with the rest of the house rather than a patched-over opening. Materials, window proportions and detailing often make the difference.

rules.permitted_development: A garage conversion will often avoid planning permission where the work is internal and the building is not enlarged. That is much less likely if the conversion creates a separate dwelling, relies on an extension or sits on an estate where parking or garage retention was controlled by condition.

rules.height_rules: If the work stays within the existing garage shell there is no new height allowance to use. Raising the roof, adding an upper floor or rebuilding the garage turns it into an extension or new outbuilding question rather than a straightforward conversion.
rules.depth_rules: There is no separate garage-conversion depth right. The simplest case is an internal fit-out within the existing footprint; once the scheme projects outward, adds a link or enlarges the building, the normal extension rules or a planning application come into play.
rules.boundary_rules: Check the planning history for parking-retention or estate conditions, and review any side-boundary or road-facing changes carefully. A new window, door or infill wall close to neighbours can still raise amenity and design issues.
rules.roof_rules: A simple internal conversion does not create a fresh roof allowance. If the project also alters the roof, adds dormers or changes the ridge or eaves profile, that element needs its own planning assessment.
rules.materials_rules: Any infill where the garage door is removed should look deliberate and sit comfortably with the house. Matching brickwork, openings and detailing usually helps, but listed building or conservation controls can still override the ordinary route.

rules.roof_rules: A simple internal conversion does not create a fresh roof allowance. If the project also alters the roof, adds dormers or changes the ridge or eaves profile, that element needs its own planning assessment.
rules.materials_rules: Any infill where the garage door is removed should look deliberate and sit comfortably with the house. Matching brickwork, openings and detailing usually helps, but listed building or conservation controls can still override the ordinary route.

rules.permitted_development: Planning permission is not usually needed for a straightforward internal garage conversion, but enlarging the structure, changing the outside materially or creating separate living accommodation can move it outside the ordinary householder route.

rules.height_rules: Garage conversion does not create a fresh height allowance. The moment the scheme raises the roofline, adds a storey or materially rebuilds the structure, it needs to be assessed as extension or outbuilding development instead.
rules.depth_rules: A conversion inside the existing garage envelope is usually the easiest case. If the proposal extends the garage, pushes the front line out or adds linked built form, use the normal extension framework rather than assuming the conversion still stands alone.
rules.boundary_rules: The key local checks are often parking retention, frontage design and neighbour-facing openings. Even a simple garage-door infill can become a planning issue where earlier conditions controlled parking or the altered elevation is prominent.
rules.roof_rules: Garage conversion by itself does not open a separate roof right. Any proposal to lift, rebuild or materially alter the garage roof should be treated as external development in its own right.
rules.materials_rules: When a garage door is replaced, aim for an elevation that belongs with the rest of the house rather than a patched-over opening. Materials, window proportions and detailing often make the difference.

rules.permitted_development: The simplest garage conversion is an internal fit-out within the existing shell, which often does not need planning permission. The position changes quickly if the building is enlarged, rebuilt as part of the scheme or intended to operate as a separate home. This authority also records an Article 4 direction or another local removal of rights, so check the planning history before relying on the simpler route.

rules.height_rules: A pure conversion works within the existing envelope, so there is no separate garage-conversion height right. Once the roof is lifted, rebuilt or given an extra storey, treat that element as new external development.
rules.depth_rules: Depth is not the main test for a garage conversion. Staying within the existing footprint is the low-risk route, whereas any outward projection, linked enlargement or rebuild has to be considered under extension rules or a full planning route.
rules.boundary_rules: Boundary and frontage issues usually come from the external alterations rather than the internal fit-out. Also check whether an earlier permission required the garage or parking space to be retained as part of the approved layout.
rules.roof_rules: Roof changes are not part of the ordinary internal conversion question. Once the scheme includes a raised roof, dormer, rooflights on a sensitive elevation or other visible roof alteration, assess that work separately.
rules.materials_rules: The external treatment of a former garage opening matters more than the internal fit-out. A well-matched infill wall, window or entrance usually reads best, especially on a principal or street-facing elevation.
